claims.feature: other: history as residue on ordinary lives
claims.claim: Kay says Children of Earth and Sky was deliberately about people who are not important in the scheme of things, and about how grand events can reach down and affect people far away.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Children of Earth and Sky Author Questions, BrightWeavings
claims.quote: how those grand events can reach down and affect people far away

claims.claim: Kay says he declined a Fernand Braudel passage as an epigraph because it felt too on the nose as to one theme.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Children of Earth and Sky: An Origin Story', BrightWeavings
claims.quote: it felt too ‘on the nose’ as to one theme

claims.claim: Kay says he prefers epigraphs of association, ones that open up more after a reader has finished a book.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Children of Earth and Sky: An Origin Story', BrightWeavings

claims.claim: Kay says the Provence landmarks he stumbled on, among them a round roofless medieval watchtower in the middle of nowhere, started a different sort of tale telling itself to him.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Letter to the Reader of Ysabel'
claims.quote: a round, roofless medieval watchtower in the middle of nowhere

claims.feature: other: history as residue on a place
claims.claim: Kay says he began thinking about how some parts of the world still carry the hard imprint of what has gone before.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Letter to the Reader of Ysabel'
claims.quote: still carry the hard imprint of what has gone before

claims.feature: other: research must be digested not dumped
claims.claim: Kay says his grounding in research has to be so secure that the vast majority of it does not enter the book except subliminally or very quietly, or else the result is the info dump he hates as a reader.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Kristin Centorcelli, SF Signal
claims.quote: does not enter the book except subliminally, or does so very quietly
claims.page: answer on research for River of Stars

claims.feature: other: minor figures carry the setting
claims.claim: Kay says he often achieves his strongest effects through the peripheral figures, whether of character, emotion, or shaping depth to a setting for the reader.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Kristin Centorcelli, SF Signal
claims.quote: through the peripheral figures I can achieve my strongest effects

claims.claim: Kay says he uses what he calls the porter in Macbeth idea, holding back the revelation of something or the moving forward of the main plot, to heighten drama.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Kristin Centorcelli, SF Signal
claims.quote: holding back the revelation of something, or the moving forward

claims.claim: Kay says the principal reason the language of the Fionavar trilogy differs from his later books is that Fionavar was his mythic endeavour while the later books track a movement towards history.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Afterword to the HarperPerennial Canada 20th anniversary edition of The Fionavar Tapestry
claims.quote: the language of the trilogy differs from my later books

claims.claim: Kay says the language of Fionavar was guided by the matter of the book, a god imprisoned under a mountain and a wolf and dog fighting beneath a sacrificial tree.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword (2003)
claims.quote: Language was guided by that context

claims.claim: Kay says he imagined the narrative arc of Fionavar in operatic terms, moving from aria to aria.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword (2003)
claims.quote: in operatic terms, moving from aria to aria

claims.claim: Kay says he has joked that the scale of Fionavar was built so that he could write the sentence 'Rain, rain, rain, rain, rain' for Paul on the Summer Tree.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword (2003)

claims.claim: Kay says he does not believe in saying exactly what happens to characters after a novel closes, and that the ending of every book he has written makes this point.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword (2003)
claims.quote: saying exactly what happens to characters after a novel closes

claims.claim: Kay says he cut a planned Sharra scene because it felt static and flat and was in the book only to tie up a thread he did not think was really loose.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword (2003)

claims.claim: Kay says an exile experiencing a new place gives the reader a way in, because that character's observations and reactions serve a reader who is also away from home.
claims.quote: their observations and reactions become a way in for the reader
